turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale, quick vitals before you go in. Blood pressure is one forty-eight over ninety-two, heart rate seventy-eight, oxygen saturation ninety-seven percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I appreciate you telling me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Parking was impossible today. We circled the garage twice.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): One second, this thing just logged me out. Okay. What brings you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, Doctor. I have come about a cough that will not go away, and I thought it best to have it checked.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): A cough? Sorry, a box popped up. Would you say that again?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly. A cough. It has been quite persistent.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Ellen, his wife. Dry cough, and it keeps him up at night. He keeps blaming a cold.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been there?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It has been two weeks. Pardon me, I misspoke. It has been three weeks.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not three. Six weeks. It was going before his brother came down from Ohio.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between three and six weeks. Can either of you give me the actual start date?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid I cannot give a precise date.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the cough dry, or are you bringing up phlegm?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): It is dry. I am not bringing up any phlegm.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I have not had a fever.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath? Wheezing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No shortness of breath, and no wheezing.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He did have a head cold at the start. Runny nose, some sneezing. That's finished.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The nasal congestion cleared after a few days. The cough remained. I had connected the cough to that cold.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): It does seem worse when I lie down, if that detail is helpful.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): It is. Let me listen. Lungs are clear, no crackles, and the heart sounds are regular.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are you taking for the blood pressure? Slowly, please, I'm still in the chart.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I was started on ramipril. The dose is five milligrams — no, forgive me, it is ten milligrams, once every morning.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams of ramipril. One more time? The cursor jumped.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams of ramipril, by mouth, every morning. It was begun for my high blood pressure.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He misses doses. Last week he skipped two mornings while we were away.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): That is true, regrettably. I did miss those two doses.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else besides that?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I also take the water tablet. A small white tablet. I am not certain of the proper name.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): The water tablet — do you know the strength? I didn't catch a number.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I believe it may be twenty-five milligrams, but I would not swear to that.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His sister takes lisinopril, ten milligrams, and she coughed for months. I wondered if this was the same thing.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's the sister's lisinopril, not yours. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have no known allergies.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): You've got hypertension, and one forty-eight over ninety-two is still up. I'm thinking the cough could be from the ramipril, though I would not call that definite.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll order a chest x-ray today, and we'll leave the ramipril alone for now.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cough really took off right after the ramipril was started. I said that at the time.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I defer to you, of course, but the timing does appear to match the new medicine.

[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): That changes it. Cancel the x-ray for today. I was about to switch you to lisinopril, but that's the same kind of drug, so no. We'll stop the ramipril and start losartan, fifty milligrams once a day, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): We might do a chest x-ray if the cough has not settled in two weeks.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I keep taking the water tablet?

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep the water tablet as you have been, and bring the bottle so we can read the name. Come back in two weeks so I can recheck the pressure and the cough. If you get chest pain, a fever, or you can't catch your breath, go to the emergency room rather than waiting.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I'll have your paperwork at the desk. Drive safe.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Dry current cough, worse lying down supported; duration is uncertain range summarized by doctor, not patient/certain.
bad.text: dry cough (category=respiratory, status=present, duration=approximately 3 to 6 weeks, temporality=current, aggravating_factors=lying down, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Sneezing resolved is mentioned by family member, not patient.
Current water tablet supported, but 25 mg is uncertain, not definite.

omissions.text: Initial associated upper respiratory symptoms were a head cold with runny nose; this was not recorded, while sneezing was attributed to the patient rather than the family member.
The cough keeps him up at night / is worse at night, reported by the wife; this key detail is not captured as a cough feature, only as generic difficulty sleeping.
Medication adherence detail: the patient missed two morning doses of ramipril last week while away.
The water tablet dose of 25 mg was explicitly uncertain ('I believe it may be 25 milligrams, but I would not swear to that'); recording it as 25 mg without uncertainty is inaccurate.
The doctor initially planned a chest x-ray that day, then cancelled it after the history suggested ramipril-related cough; this cancellation/change in plan is not recorded.
The doctor stated he was about to switch the patient to lisinopril but decided against it because it is the same class of drug; this medication plan change is not recorded.
Follow-up purpose was to recheck both blood pressure and cough in two weeks, not just a generic follow-up consultation.
